question: What are the candidate therapeutic targets, immune pathways and biomarkers in ulcerative colitis with the strongest convergent evidence?

models.orchestrator: Claude Opus 5.5 — Claude Code main session
models.agents: Claude Sonnet 5.5 — Claude Code subagents (agente-expresion, agente-literatura, agente-externo, agente-celular, agente-vias, agente-aplicado)

findings.statement: CXCR2 tops the convergence ranking: up in UC in all five cohorts, meta-analysis log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264], and higher in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient (paired log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6972]). It has genetic and tractability support (CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists in clinical trials), but the bulk signal very likely reflects infiltrating neutrophils, so cell composition must be checked.

CXCL8, the neutrophil chemokine ligand of CXCR1 and CXCR2, is strongly and reproducibly up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.7037]) and is enriched in inflamed mucosa; it supports a neutrophil-recruitment axis (CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCR1, CXCR2 all up). Part of the signal comes from infiltrating myeloid cells, not only epithelium.

OSMR is up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=OSMR; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.042]) and local to inflamed mucosa (paired inflamed vs non-inflamed log2FC [gene=OSMR; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=0.8848]); it combines genetic association with an existing drug (vixarelimab) and fits the OSM/OSMR axis, expressed mainly by stromal cells.

HMGCS2, an epithelial ketogenesis and metabolism gene, is lost in UC in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845]). It is unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa versus control (log2FC [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=-0.0649]), so the loss marks local inflammation rather than the underlying disease. It is a biomarker, not a plausible target.

CHI3L1 has one of the largest and most reproducible increases (meta log2FC [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.7135]; up in all five cohorts). It is also modestly raised in non-inflamed MSCCR mucosa (log2FC [gene=CHI3L1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.8377]), so it reflects both local inflammation and a disease-level shift. It is a strong biomarker candidate with no approved drug.

JAK2 ranks high mainly through genetics and tractability; its expression change is small (meta log2FC [gene=JAK2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=0.872]). This is a modest, broadly replicated rise, not a strong transcriptional marker; the target case rests on genetics and existing JAK inhibitors, not on expression magnitude.

DUOX2 (with its maturation factor DUOXA2) is among the largest epithelial increases, up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.3213]) and clearly higher in inflamed mucosa of the same patient. It points to epithelial oxidative and antimicrobial stress and is a biomarker candidate, not a drugged target.

S100A8 (with S100A9, the calprotectin pair) is up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.6467]) and enriched in inflamed mucosa. This is largely a neutrophil and myeloid signal, consistent with calprotectin as a stool biomarker; the bulk increase may reflect infiltration rather than tissue-intrinsic change.

CD274 (PD-L1) is up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=CD274; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=1.887]) with genetic support; it looks like an interferon-driven, inflammation-induced regulatory feedback program, probably partly from immune cells, and is not an obvious inhibition target.

IDO1 is strongly up in all five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.445]) and higher in inflamed mucosa, consistent with an interferon-gamma tryptophan-catabolism response. It has IDO1 inhibitors in oncology but no genetic support, and the immune-cell contribution is unresolved.

CLDN8, a tight-junction gene, is the strongest meta-analysis decrease (meta log2FC [gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.5181]; down in all five cohorts) and is lower in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa. Like other lost epithelial genes (SLC26A2, PCK1, AQP8), it indicates barrier and absorptive-epithelium loss, so it is a biomarker, not a target.

REG1A is strongly up and local to inflamed mucosa, but its replication is weaker than for the other top genes: it is not significant in the Leuven infliximab cohort GSE16879 (padj [gene=REG1A; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE16879; layer=rna; cohort=GSE16879; contrast=uc_vs_control; padj=0.132]), so four of five cohorts agree.

caveats: Heterogeneity across cohorts is high for most top genes (I2 near or above 0.9), so effect sizes differ between RNA-seq and microarrays; compare directions and significance, not magnitudes.
The four microarray cohorts have small control groups (12 to 21 controls, 18 in UNIFI).

Bulk expression cannot separate tissue-intrinsic change from neutrophil and myeloid infiltration; this affects CXCR1/2, CXCL8, S100A8/9, IDO1, CD274, MMPs and IL1B. Cell-composition analysis is needed.
Convergence scores for genetics, literature and tractability come from Open Targets and the knowledge graph, not from this expression data.
The data are cross-sectional biopsy transcriptomes; they do not show causality or therapeutic response.

findings.statement: CXCR2 ranks first in the convergence ranking and has clinical-stage antagonists (reparixin Phase 3, navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682 Phase 2) in Open Targets, but the corpus holds no extracted literature relations for it. The only literature support is a hub-gene listing of CXCR2 among hub genes in active UC (with MMP-9, CHI3L1, CXCL9, CXCL10, S100A9). The therapeutic case rests on expression and genetics, not on UC-specific trials.

The literature states that the axis of CXCL8 with its receptors CXCR1 and CXCR2 participates in UC pathogenesis via PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signaling. CXCL8 was also a hub gene in a PPI analysis and a blood diagnostic marker for IBD in a validation cohort. This is mechanistic and bioinformatic support, not interventional evidence in UC. It supports this CXCL8 neutrophil axis as a coherent target module.

A single study reports that IDO1 is elevated in UC and induces pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization via the GRP78-XBP1 ER-stress pathway. A methyl-tryptophan IDO1 inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis in mice. Evidence is preclinical and from one group. Approved or clinical IDO1 inhibitors exist for oncology, not for UC.

CHI3L1 is upregulated in UC and correlates with NLRP3 inflammasome expression. It is reported to promote macrophage pyroptosis via a BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis, and its inhibition was protective. Velpatasvir binds recombinant CHI3L1 in vitro, a repurposing hypothesis only. No approved CHI3L1 drug exists. The support comes from single, recent studies.

MMP1 is described as having strong diagnostic potential in a bioinformatic study of UC-associated CRC. Its transcript is modified by mirikizumab and correlates with Mayo, Geboes and Robarts indices. It also associates with macrophage infiltration. It is part of a five-mRNA anti-TNF response panel (with IL13RA2, HCAR3, CSF3, INHBA) in a prospective ML study, so it is a candidate response and activity marker, not a validated one.

DUOX2 is among the proteins most elevated in inflamed UC biopsies relative to healthy controls. It was named among credible diagnostic biomarkers (with S100A8, IL1B, CXCL1, MMP10 and others). One study reports that a herbal formula (TLXDS) alleviates colitis by inhibiting DUOX2 overexpression, with a ferroptosis link. This is mostly signature-level and preclinical evidence, and DUOX2 has no drug.

S100A9 expression is reported to diagnose active UC with excellent ROC performance, and it is higher in UC by ONT-RNA-seq. In tofacitinib-treated patients, response was associated with S100A9 downregulation in resident macrophages. This suggests S100A9 tracks response and possibly a myeloid source rather than an epithelial change.

AQP9 is expressed predominantly in neutrophils (single-cell and immunofluorescence) and is upregulated in mouse UC colon. It is reported to promote NET formation via JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis and to injure the epithelium. This is mouse-based work with no AQP9 drug in Open Targets. The signal is neutrophil-derived and not a change in the epithelium itself.

LCN2 is higher in UC than in controls, and decreases from short-duration UC to long-duration UC to UC-associated cancer. It is proposed as a diagnostic marker of UC-associated carcinogenesis tied to disease duration. This is a single-study finding.

OSMR has no extracted literature relations here, despite strong expression and replication support and the vixarelimab drug record. Mirikizumab treatment altered transcripts tied to resistance to current therapies, including IL1B, OSMR, FCGR3A/B and CXCL6, which suggests that OSMR is involved in anti-TNF and JAK-inhibitor resistance.

Tofacitinib is approved for moderate-to-severe UC, yet only a minority of patients respond in the cited tofacitinib cohort, and its mechanisms are described as unknown. JAK2 has no extracted literature relations in this corpus. It appears only as a downstream mediator in AQP9-driven neutrophil NET formation (JAK2-STAT3).

CXCR1 has no extracted literature relations. It is linked to the CXCL8 neutrophil axis through the CXCL8 pathogenesis sentence, so it should be read as the same neutrophil module as CXCR2, not as independent literature support.

A neutrophil-centered molecular subtype of UC exists, defined by ferroptosis and neutrophil gene sets. This frames the neutrophil genes (CXCR1, CXCR2, CXCL8, AQP9, S100A8, S100A9, LCN2) as one cell-type signal that may reflect infiltrating cells, not changes in the tissue itself.

caveats: No numeric values are cited because the cited records did not need numbers. Strengths are described qualitatively.

Many top-ranked genes (CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274, FCGR2A, JAK2, IL2RA, OSMR, PI3, CXCL5, REG1A, CDH3, DUOXA2) have no extracted literature relations in this corpus; their support comes from expression and Open Targets only.

Most literature support is bioinformatic hub-gene or signature work or single mouse studies; few trial-level data exist in the corpus. I did not search CD274, IL1B, NOS2, MMP9 or the metabolic downregulated genes (SLC26A2, HMGCS2) in depth.
Neutrophil and macrophage genes may reflect infiltrating cells rather than epithelial change.

findings.statement: CXCR2 is the top-ranked convergence gene: it is up in UC biopsies (meta-analysis log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264]) and has strong Open Targets genetic support ([gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.8171]). It is tractable (small molecule: advanced clinical) with reparixin at PHASE_3 and several other antagonists at PHASE_2 (none is a UC-approved drug).

Reactome places CXCR2 in neutrophil degranulation, chemokine receptors binding chemokines and G alpha(i) signalling. STRING high-confidence partners are the ELR+ chemokines CXCL8, CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCL2, CXCL6, CXCL3 plus PPBP and CXCR1, defining a neutrophil-recruitment axis.

CXCR1 is the second-ranked gene, up in biopsies ([gene=CXCR1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=1.769]) with genetic and drug support shared with CXCR2 (reparixin PHASE_3, ladarixin, navarixin, SX-682 at PHASE_2). It is probably co-targeted with CXCR2 by the same antagonists.

CXCL8 is strongly up ([gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.704]) and replicates in five cohorts, but it has no Open Targets genetic association signal (genetics component zero in the ranking); its drugs are ABX-IL8 and adakitug, both PHASE_2. Expression-led and literature-led, not genetically supported.

IL23R has very strong genetic association ([gene=IL23R; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.9411]) but barely changes in biopsies ([gene=IL23R; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-0.292]), so it ranks well below the top fifty of the target profile and is not in the convergence top. A genetically supported gene that expression does not capture (IL23 pathway drugs act upstream via IL12B/IL23A).

CHI3L1 is among the most up-regulated genes ([gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.714]) and replicates in five cohorts, but it has no known drug and no genetic association; it is a biomarker candidate rather than a drug target. The same expression-only, undrugged profile applies to DUOX2, AQP9, S100A8/S100A9, LCN2 and CXCL1.

IDO1 is strongly induced ([gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.445]) with no genetic association; Open Targets lists epacadostat (max stage APPROVAL as returned) and linrodostat (PHASE_3), both from other indications, so repurposing is a hypothesis only.

OSMR combines up-regulation ([gene=OSMR; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.042]) with Open Targets genetic support and an antibody (vixarelimab, PHASE_2, antibody tractability advanced clinical); its Reactome pathway is IL-6-type cytokine receptor ligand interactions.

JAK2 has a high Open Targets UC score ([gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318]) but only a modest biopsy change ([gene=JAK2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=0.872]); drugs listed (e.g. fedratinib, approval) are in other indications.

FCGR2A has strong genetic association ([gene=FCGR2A; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.87]) with a small expression change and no listed drug; the signal likely reflects infiltrating myeloid cells.

CD274 (PD-L1) is up in biopsies ([gene=CD274; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=1.887]) and has approved antibodies from oncology (e.g. atezolizumab, PHASE_4); an agonist-direction hypothesis in UC is untested here, since existing drugs block the pathway.

MMP1 is strongly up ([gene=MMP1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.661]) without genetic support; marimastat and doxycycline are listed but are broad MMP inhibitors, so MMP1, MMP3, MMP7 and MMP10 are better read as tissue-damage biomarkers.

caveats: Established UC targets TNF and JAK1 are not in the stored convergence, target or biomarker rankings, so the ranking favours up-regulated genes over drug targets whose expression is unchanged.
Drug stages are from Open Targets in any indication; none of the CXCR2 or IDO1 drugs is shown to be approved for UC.
Only CXCR2, OSMR and CD274 target profiles were queried directly; other drug and tractability details come from the convergence ranking records.
Open Targets genetic association was zero or absent for most of the strongest expression-led genes, which says nothing about causality.

findings.statement: CXCR2, the top-ranked candidate, is almost entirely a neutrophil transcript in Gubatan 2026 (neutrophil share [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]). Smillie 2019 did not capture neutrophils and assigns it to T/NK cells, so the attribution does not replicate there (replicated=false; second dataset says myeloid). In bulk the change shrinks from [gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; unadjusted_log2fc=2.5984] to [gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4409], still significant, so the verdict is partly_composition: the bulk signal is mostly neutrophil influx, with a smaller residual that may reflect over-correction.

CXCL8 is made mainly by neutrophils in inflamed mucosa (neutrophil share [gene=CXCL8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.873]), while Smillie 2019 attributes it to macrophages and a second dataset agrees on myeloid lineage. After composition adjustment it is no longer significant ([gene=CXCL8; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_padj=0.0527]), verdict composition. It behaves as a marker of myeloid and neutrophil influx; this is not proof of pure influx because adjustment can over-correct.

IL1B is myeloid in both datasets, but neutrophils carry a large share of its inflamed-tissue transcripts ([gene=IL1B; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.702]). Its bulk increase does not survive composition adjustment ([gene=IL1B; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_padj=0.0735]), verdict composition, so it is mainly a cell-influx marker; the caveat on over-correction applies.

S100A8 is a myeloid transcript replicated across datasets, with most inflamed-mucosa transcripts coming from neutrophils ([gene=S100A8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.909]). It keeps a significant adjusted change ([gene=S100A8; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.9231]), verdict partly_composition: a neutrophil and monocyte burden marker with some within-tissue induction.

CD274 (PD-L1) is spread across lineages (myeloid dominant in Smillie, replicated in the second dataset) with a large neutrophil share in Gubatan ([gene=CD274; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.687]). It retains a significant adjusted change ([gene=CD274; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4978]), verdict partly_composition: a mixed influx and tissue induction signal, not a clean single-cell target.

IDO1 is myeloid (macrophages and DC1, replicated in the second dataset) and not a neutrophil gene (neutrophil share [gene=IDO1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.072]); in Gubatan enterocytes are also a top source. The adjusted change stays significant ([gene=IDO1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8505]), verdict partly_composition, which points to induction inside the tissue.

MMP1 is a stromal product, replicated in the second dataset, led by inflammatory fibroblasts in inflamed mucosa (cluster share [gene=MMP1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; top_clusters_inflamed.0.share=0.531]). The change keeps strong significance after adjustment ([gene=MMP1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.2636]), verdict partly_composition, so it is a fibroblast-state change inside the tissue rather than neutrophil influx.

CHI3L1 is mainly an inflammatory-fibroblast gene (cluster share [gene=CHI3L1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; top_clusters_inflamed.0.share=0.652]), replicated in the second dataset, although neutrophil states also contribute in Gubatan. The adjusted change remains large ([gene=CHI3L1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3967]), verdict partly_composition, supporting a tissue-intrinsic fibroblast signal.

DUOX2 is epithelial (enterocytes and immature enterocytes), replicated in the second dataset, with an epithelial lineage share of [gene=DUOX2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.947] and almost no neutrophil contribution. Its adjusted change stays significant ([gene=DUOX2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3161]), verdict partly_composition: an epithelial-intrinsic induction and a sign of epithelial stress.

OSMR is stromal (lineage share [gene=OSMR; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.907], replicated in the second dataset), spread over several fibroblast clusters. The adjusted change is small but still significant ([gene=OSMR; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.2528]), verdict partly_composition, so most of the bulk rise tracks cell composition and only a modest part is intrinsic.

caveats: No candidate in the tested set received the verdict intrinsic; most were partly_composition, and CXCL8 and IL1B were composition.
Composition adjustment can over-correct, because lineage scores also rise when resident cells activate; losing significance is not proof of pure influx, and keeping it is the stronger statement.
Smillie 2019 lacks neutrophils, so neutrophil-derived genes (CXCR2, CXCR1, CXCL8, S100A8, AQP9) are attributed to other immune cells there; use the Gubatan neutrophil shares for them.
Shares compare cell types, not tissue abundance; dissociation protocols enrich some fractions.
CXCR1, AQP9, CXCL1, MMP3, LCN2 and SLC26A2 were only screened for neutrophil share (CXCR1 and AQP9 are mostly neutrophil, SLC26A2 almost none); no composition analysis was run for them.
Spatial context (Xenium) was not examined within the call budget.

findings.statement: TNFa and NFkB are the most uniformly and strongly activated PROGENy pathways in inflamed UC mucosa (up in five of five cohorts); TNFa reaches its highest t in GSE206285 [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=20.07]. This fits the established anti-TNF target but is a broad inflammatory readout.

JAK-STAT pathway activity is up in five of five cohorts, for example in GSE193677 [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE193677.t=15.68]. This is consistent with the approved JAK inhibitor class.

STAT3 regulon activity is up in five of five cohorts, for example in GSE206285 [type=tf_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=24.0]. It is the central JAK-STAT effector; activity is inferred from target genes, not from STAT3 mRNA.

EGFR, MAPK, PI3K, TGFb, hypoxia, VEGF and estrogen pathways are also up in five of five cohorts, and the top TF list is dominated by stress and AP1/ATF family members (AP1 in GSE193677 [type=tf_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE193677.t=18.4]). These are non-specific: inflamed mucosa activates many programs at once, so they are weak for target prioritisation compared with specific circuits.

p53 pathway activity is down in three of five cohorts and not up in any (GSE16879 [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE16879.t=-3.59]), so it is not a consistent signature. WNT and Trail are up in four of five cohorts, not all five.

CXCR2 is rank 1 in the convergence ranking: up in five of five cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264]), with strong genetics and literature support, and with clinical-stage antagonists (reparixin Phase 3, navarixin, ladarixin and SX-682 Phase 2), none approved for UC.

In the single-cell data the CXCR2 transcript is almost entirely neutrophil-derived (neutrophil share of transcripts in inflamed mucosa [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]). Without neutrophils, as in Smillie, it maps to T/NK cells at a very low fraction of cells expressing and does not replicate. The bulk increase therefore largely reflects neutrophil infiltration, not a change of the epithelium or stroma, so CXCR2 acts as a neutrophil-recruitment target.

CXCL8 transcripts in inflamed mucosa come mainly from neutrophil states (neutrophil share of transcripts [gene=CXCL8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.873]), led by Neutrophil CXCR4, Neutrophil and Neutrophil OSM. In Smillie, which has no neutrophils, macrophages dominate, so the cell source depends on dataset capture. CXCL8 has only phase 2 anti-IL-8 antibodies (ABX-IL8, adakitug).

Circuit CXCL8 (Neutrophil CXCR4) to CXCR2 (Neutrophil) is a neutrophil-to-neutrophil loop whose co-expression score rises in inflamed UC mucosa (log2 change vs uninflamed [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.755]). Co-expression is not proof of signalling.

Neutrophil CXCL8 is also co-expressed with ACKR1 on ACKR1 endothelial cells (log2 change vs uninflamed for the generic Neutrophil sender [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=1.991]), a candidate neutrophil-to-venule recruitment axis. ACKR1 is an atypical chemokine receptor and no ACKR1-directed drug was found. Co-expression only.

IL1B from monocyte-derived macrophages is co-expressed with IL1R2 on neutrophil states (log2 change vs uninflamed for Neutrophil CXCR4 as receiver [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.059]). IL1R2 is a decoy receptor, so this score does not imply signalling. IL1B is drug-tractable (canakinumab approved in other indications) but has no UC approval.

Negative result: the neutrophil-OSM to IL6ST on LP fibroblast circuit has a low score in inflamed mucosa and falls versus uninflamed (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=-0.709]). The Gubatan data do not support a strong neutrophil OSM to inflammatory fibroblast signal. The only increase is Neutrophil PADI4 to LP fibroblast, from a zero baseline score.

CHI3L1 is among the strongest replicated up-regulated genes (meta log2FC [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.7135], five of five cohorts) and has no drug, as is also true of AQP9, DUOX2 and CXCL1 in the top-ranked list. It is better framed as a biomarker or undrugged candidate than a validated target.

caveats: PROGENy and CollecTRI activities are inferred from bulk biopsies; shifts in cell composition (neutrophil and macrophage infiltration) can drive them and cannot be separated from within-cell signalling.
Ligand-receptor scores are co-expression of mean CP10K, not evidence of signalling; IL1R2 is a decoy receptor and ACKR1 is atypical.
Bulk cohort comparisons are inflamed or UC versus control, whereas communication scores compare inflamed with uninflamed UC mucosa in one single-cell dataset (Gubatan 2026).
Neutrophils are absent from Smillie 2019, so cell-source calls for neutrophil genes (CXCL8, CXCR2) depend on the dataset used.
IL-23 and integrin pathways were not directly assessed because PROGENy has no such pathway; JAK-STAT and TNFa activity are the proxies for approved drug classes.
Pathways active in five cohorts include many non-specific programs; specific circuits are preferred.

findings.statement: Baseline NFkB pathway activity is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000484]), but it is equally associated with non-response in the UNIFI placebo arm (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.00608]), so this marks severity rather than a drug-specific mechanism. TNFa behaves the same way, significant in all four drug arms and UNIFI placebo.

In the PURSUIT placebo arm the NFkB association with non-response is absent (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (PURSUIT).padj=0.932]); that arm is small, so the lack of signal is weak evidence.

JAK-STAT activity is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0124]) but does not reach significance for golimumab (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.golimumab.padj=0.204]); it is also nominally higher in UNIFI placebo non-responders, so severity contributes.

TGFb pathway activity is associated with ustekinumab non-response (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.000493]) but not golimumab non-response (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.golimumab.padj=0.348]); UNIFI placebo is also significant, so it is not clearly drug-specific.

Baseline OSM is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (BH padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000264]), but the drug-vs-placebo interaction is null (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; interaction.ustekinumab.padj=0.971]) and UNIFI placebo is similar in direction (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.116]). Nothing survives correction in golimumab, infliximab or vedolizumab, so OSM looks like a severity marker rather than a ustekinumab-specific one.

TREM1 is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (BH padj [gene=TREM1; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000474]) and also in UNIFI placebo non-responders (BH padj [gene=TREM1; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0234]), consistent with severity; the other biologic arms do not survive correction.

IL11 shows the strongest ustekinumab association among the genes tested (BH padj [gene=IL11; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=3.68e-8]), but it also separates UNIFI placebo non-responders (BH padj [gene=IL11; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0133]), and the interaction test is not significant, so it marks severity.

CXCR2 is the top convergence candidate (meta-analysis log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264], up in five cohorts, with clinical-stage antagonists). Its baseline level is associated with ustekinumab non-response (BH padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=9.69e-6]) but equally with UNIFI placebo non-response (BH padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0126]), so the response signal is severity-linked and likely neutrophil-driven.

CXCL8 is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (BH padj [gene=CXCL8; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.000102]) and in UNIFI placebo non-responders (BH padj [gene=CXCL8; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0154]); no golimumab, infliximab or vedolizumab difference survives correction.

Baseline IL23A, the ustekinumab target pathway, is not associated with ustekinumab response (BH padj [gene=IL23A; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.977]); target expression does not mark response.
Baseline ITGB7, the vedolizumab target subunit, is not associated with vedolizumab response (BH padj [gene=ITGB7; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.vedolizumab.padj=0.995]).

LAX1 is the top first-in-class candidate (up in five cohorts, antibody-tractable) but is flagged partly composition-driven, with only a fraction retained after composition adjustment (retained [gene=LAX1; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.23]). Single-cell data place it mainly in plasma cells and T cells, so the signal largely reflects infiltrating immune cells and the second dataset does not replicate the T/NK lineage.

XKR9 is epithelial-intrinsic but replicated in only a small number of cohorts (cohorts up [gene=XKR9; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; cohorts_up=2]), few cells express it, and the second dataset points to plasma cells, so support is thin.

SDR16C5 is the cleanest epithelial candidate, with most of its signal retained after composition adjustment (retained [gene=SDR16C5; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.66]) and the epithelial lineage confirmed in the second dataset. Missing are functional or genetic support and any response-cohort data.

CHRDL2 is stromal, mainly inflammatory fibroblasts, with the lineage replicated in the second dataset, but it has appreciable RNA in a vital organ (max HPA nTPM [gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; vital_max_ntpm=42.6]) and is partly composition-driven, which is a safety flag to resolve.

ADGRG3 is classed as a first-in-class opportunity, but its transcripts are almost entirely neutrophil-derived (neutrophil share [gene=ADGRG3; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; neutrophil_share=0.906]), so it is a neutrophil-abundance readout rather than a tissue-intrinsic change.

caveats: Response cohorts are small except UNIFI ustekinumab; infliximab and vedolizumab arms have few responders, so the lack of significance there is not evidence of absence.
Many ustekinumab associations match the UNIFI placebo arm and the drug-vs-placebo interaction is null for the genes tested, so they reflect severity, not drug-specific mechanism.
Associations are baseline, bulk-tissue and cross-sectional; they are not predictions and need prospective validation.
The discovery screen is bulk plus single-cell derived and has no functional or genetic validation; neutrophils are absent from the Smillie dataset.
Only the first few discovery candidates were profiled.

summary.text: The candidate with the strongest convergent evidence is the neutrophil chemokine receptor CXCR2, first in the deterministic ranking. It is up in all five biopsy cohorts (meta-analysis log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264]), has strong Open Targets genetic support ([gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.8171]) and clinical-stage antagonists (reparixin at Phase 3; navarixin, ladarixin and SX-682 at Phase 2), none approved for UC. Single-cell data show that its transcript is almost entirely neutrophil-derived (neutrophil share [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]), so CXCR2 is best read as a target for blocking neutrophil recruitment, whose bulk rise mostly measures neutrophil influx rather than a change of resident tissue.

The most robust tissue-intrinsic changes come from inflammatory fibroblasts and epithelium, not from infiltrating cells. MMP1 and CHI3L1 are inflammatory-fibroblast genes and DUOX2 an epithelial gene, and all three keep large changes after adjustment for cell composition (adjusted log2FC [gene=MMP1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.2636], [gene=CHI3L1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3967] and [gene=DUOX2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3161]) with the cell-type attribution replicated in a second single-cell dataset. None has genetic support or a UC drug, so they are the strongest tissue biomarkers and hypotheses for new targets, not validated targets.

The largest decreases describe loss of differentiated absorptive and metabolic epithelium: the tight-junction gene CLDN8 ([gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.5181]) and the ketogenic enzyme HMGCS2 ([gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845]) are down in all five cohorts. HMGCS2 is unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa of the same cohort ([gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=-0.0649]), so these losses mark local inflammation and are biomarkers, not targets.

At the pathway level TNFa, NFkB and JAK-STAT activity are raised in inflamed mucosa in all five cohorts (TNFa in UNIFI [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=20.07]); these are the axes of the approved anti-TNF and JAK-inhibitor classes and act as positive controls. Baseline genes associated with ustekinumab non-response, including OSM, mostly separate placebo non-responders as well, and the drug-versus-placebo interaction for OSM is null (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; interaction.ustekinumab.padj=0.971]), so they mark disease severity rather than drug-specific resistance.

Two limits of the convergence view matter. Genetically anchored UC genes whose mucosal expression barely changes, such as IL23R ([gene=IL23R; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.9411]), are under-ranked because the score rewards expression. Among first-in-class candidates, SDR16C5 is the cleanest epithelial hypothesis (retained after composition adjustment [gene=SDR16C5; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.66]), whereas LAX1 and ADGRG3 largely reflect infiltrating plasma cells, T cells or neutrophils.

expression.text: The random-effects meta-analysis across five cohorts (MSCCR RNA-seq and four microarray cohorts: UNIFI, PURSUIT, and two Leuven cohorts) gives a consistent picture of UC mucosa. The largest and most reproducible increases are in genes of inflammatory fibroblasts, epithelial stress and myeloid cells: CHI3L1 ([gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.7135]), the calprotectin subunit S100A8 ([gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.6467]), the epithelial oxidase DUOX2 ([gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.3213]) and the neutrophil chemokine CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.7037]), each up in all five cohorts. With the matrix metalloproteinases (MMP1, MMP3, MMP7, MMP10), LCN2 and PI3, this is an antimicrobial, tissue-remodelling and neutrophil-recruitment program.

The strongest decreases describe loss of the differentiated colonocyte: the tight-junction gene CLDN8 is the largest meta-analysis decrease ([gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.5181]), followed by the ketogenic enzyme HMGCS2 ([gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845]) and the sulfate transporter SLC26A2 ([gene=SLC26A2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.496]), all down in all five cohorts, together with ADH1C, PCK1 and AQP8. Epithelial energy metabolism (butyrate oxidation and ketogenesis), solute transport and barrier genes are lost. These genes are read-outs of epithelial injury and are biomarkers rather than therapeutic targets.

Heterogeneity between cohorts is high (for CXCR2 I2 [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; i2=0.86]), mostly because microarrays compress fold changes relative to RNA-seq, so direction and significance are more reliable than magnitude. CXCR2 is a moderate change by size ([gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264]) but ranks first because it is the only top gene that combines consistent up-regulation with genetic support and clinical-stage drugs.

inflammation.text: Comparing inflamed with non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient in MSCCR separates local from disease-wide changes. The epithelial losses are local: HMGCS2 is unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa versus controls ([gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=-0.0649]), and SLC26A2 falls sharply between paired non-inflamed and inflamed mucosa of the same patient ([gene=SLC26A2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=-1.955]). DUOX2 rises strongly with local inflammation ([gene=DUOX2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.4812]).

Some up-regulated genes are already shifted in non-inflamed mucosa, a disease-level component on top of local inflammation: CHI3L1 is modestly raised before visible inflammation ([gene=CHI3L1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.8377]). The neutrophil receptor CXCR2 instead rises mainly in the inflamed segment of the same patient ([gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6972]), as expected if it tracks neutrophil infiltration into active lesions rather than a change in resident cells.

replication.text: The changes found in the MSCCR discovery cohort reproduce well in the four microarray cohorts. Every one of the top-ranked genes discussed here is significant in the same direction in all five cohorts. For CXCR2, for example, the effect is present in UNIFI ([gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE206285; layer=rna; cohort=GSE206285; contrast=uc_vs_control; log2fc=1.7772]) and in the small Leuven infliximab cohort ([gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE16879; layer=rna; cohort=GSE16879; contrast=uc_vs_control; log2fc=3.6244]). The main exception among strong genes is REG1A, which is not significant in the Leuven infliximab cohort (padj [gene=REG1A; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE16879; layer=rna; cohort=GSE16879; contrast=uc_vs_control; padj=0.132]) and so replicates in four of five cohorts. Microarray cohorts have small control groups, which limits power for modest changes.

literature.text: Verbatim-validated literature relations support the CXCL8 neutrophil axis, which is described as participating in UC pathogenesis through PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signalling, and CXCL8 has been reported as a hub gene and a blood diagnostic marker. CHI3L1 is reported to be up in UC and to promote macrophage pyroptosis, with protective inhibition in models. MMP1 is proposed as a diagnostic and anti-TNF response marker that correlates with endoscopic and histological indices, and DUOX2 is among the proteins most elevated in inflamed biopsies. This is mechanistic, bioinformatic and preclinical support; none of it is interventional evidence in UC patients.

Literature support is uneven and partly disconnected from the ranking. CXCR2 and CXCR1 have no extracted literature relations in the corpus; CXCR2 appears only in a hub-gene list of active UC, so its rank rests on expression, genetics and drugs. IDO1 has a single preclinical study reporting that it drives pro-inflammatory macrophage polarisation and that IDO inhibition ameliorates DSS colitis. Calprotectin (S100A8 and S100A9) and LCN2 are established or proposed activity and diagnostic markers. A neutrophil-centred molecular subtype of UC has been described, which frames the neutrophil genes as one cell-type signal. AQP9, a top-ranked gene with no drug, is reported in mouse work to be a neutrophil water channel that promotes NET formation through JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis and injures the epithelium, so its rise is again neutrophil-derived.

external.text: Open Targets separates genetically anchored candidates from expression-led ones. Among the top genes, CXCR2 ([gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.8171]) and FCGR2A ([gene=FCGR2A; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.87]) have strong genetic association, and CXCR2 has clinical-stage antagonists (reparixin Phase 3, others Phase 2) shared with CXCR1. JAK2 has a high overall UC score ([gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318]) with only a modest biopsy change, consistent with the approved JAK-inhibitor class acting as a positive control. IL23R carries very strong genetics ([gene=IL23R; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; genetic_association=0.9411]) but barely changes in mucosa, so expression ranking misses it; anti-IL-23 drugs act upstream through the cytokine.

Most of the strongest expression changes have no genetic association and no UC drug. CXCL8 has only Phase 2 anti-IL-8 antibodies; IDO1 inhibitors (epacadostat, linrodostat) and CD274 antibodies come from oncology, and for CD274 existing drugs block rather than enhance an inhibitory checkpoint, the wrong direction for UC. MMP1 is reached only by broad MMP inhibitors. CHI3L1, DUOX2, AQP9, S100A8, S100A9, LCN2 and CXCL1 have no drug at all. OSMR combines up-regulation, genetic support and an antibody (vixarelimab, Phase 2). STRING places CXCR2 with the ELR-positive chemokines (CXCL8, CXCL1, CXCL5) and CXCR1 in one neutrophil-recruitment module.

cells.text: Single-cell data with neutrophils (Gubatan 2026) assign the chemokine axis to neutrophils: CXCR2 ([gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]), CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.873]) and S100A8 ([gene=S100A8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.909]) transcripts in inflamed mucosa come mostly from neutrophil states. Smillie 2019 captured no neutrophils and assigns these genes to T/NK cells or macrophages, so their attribution does not replicate there for a technical reason. IDO1 is instead myeloid (macrophages and DC1, replicated) with little neutrophil share ([gene=IDO1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.072]), and CD274 is spread across lineages.

The tissue genes come from resident cells and replicate across datasets. MMP1 ([gene=MMP1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; top_clusters_inflamed.0.share=0.531]) and CHI3L1 ([gene=CHI3L1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; top_clusters_inflamed.0.share=0.652]) are led by inflammatory fibroblasts, DUOX2 is epithelial (lineage share [gene=DUOX2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.947]) and OSMR stromal ([gene=OSMR; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.907]).

Adjusting bulk expression for cell composition separates influx from tissue change. CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_padj=0.0527]) and IL1B ([gene=IL1B; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_padj=0.0735]) lose significance (verdict composition), and CXCR2 shrinks from [gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; unadjusted_log2fc=2.5984] to [gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4409]: these neutrophil genes are mainly markers of cell influx, while CXCR2 stays a valid target of the influx itself. MMP1, CHI3L1 and DUOX2 keep large adjusted changes, and IDO1 keeps a significant one ([gene=IDO1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8505]). No gene was classed fully intrinsic, and the adjustment can over-correct when resident cells activate, so losing significance is not proof of pure influx.

pathways.text: Inferred pathway activity (PROGENy) shows TNFa and NFkB as the most uniformly activated pathways in inflamed mucosa, up in all five cohorts (TNFa in UNIFI [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=20.07]), with JAK-STAT also up in all five (MSCCR [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE193677.t=15.68]). The STAT3 regulon, the central JAK-STAT effector, is the most consistently active transcription factor ([type=tf_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=24.0]). These are the axes of approved anti-TNF and JAK-inhibitor therapy and serve as positive controls; IL-23 and integrin biology are not represented in PROGENy and could not be assessed this way.

Many other programs are also up in all five cohorts (EGFR, MAPK, PI3K, TGFb, hypoxia, VEGF), and the top transcription factors are stress and AP1 family members (AP1 in MSCCR [type=tf_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE193677.t=18.4]). Inflamed mucosa activates many programs at once, so these are weak for target prioritisation. p53 activity is down in only three cohorts ([type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE16879.t=-3.59]) and is not a consistent signature.

Among ligand-receptor circuits, the most specific is a neutrophil-to-neutrophil loop: CXCL8 from CXCR4-high neutrophils co-expressed with CXCR2 on neutrophils, whose score rises in inflamed versus uninflamed mucosa ([type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.755]); it is the axis targeted by the clinical CXCR2 antagonists. Neutrophil CXCL8 with ACKR1 on venular endothelium also rises ([type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=1.991]), a candidate recruitment axis without a drug. Macrophage IL1B with IL1R2 on neutrophils increases ([type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.059]) but IL1R2 is a decoy receptor. As a negative result, the neutrophil OSM to fibroblast IL6ST circuit falls in inflamed mucosa ([type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=-0.709]). Co-expression is not proof of signalling.

treatment.text: In baseline biopsies, inflammatory programs are associated with non-response to ustekinumab, but the same genes separate non-responders in the UNIFI placebo arm, so they mark severity rather than drug-specific resistance. NFkB activity is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000484]) and in placebo non-responders (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.00608]). The same holds for IL11 (BH padj [gene=IL11; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=3.68e-8]; placebo [gene=IL11; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0133]) and CXCR2 (BH padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=9.69e-6]; placebo [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0126]). For OSM the drug-versus-placebo interaction is null ([gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; interaction.ustekinumab.padj=0.971]).

No association for these genes survives correction in the golimumab, infliximab or vedolizumab arms, which are small, so this is weak evidence of absence; in the PURSUIT placebo arm the NFkB association is also absent (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (PURSUIT).padj=0.932]). Expression of the drug's own target does not mark response: IL23A in ustekinumab (BH padj [gene=IL23A; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.977]) and ITGB7 in vedolizumab (BH padj [gene=ITGB7; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.vedolizumab.padj=0.995]). No drug-specific response marker emerges from these data.

discovery.text: SDR16C5, a short-chain dehydrogenase, is the cleanest first-in-class hypothesis from the discovery screen. It is epithelial, the lineage is confirmed in a second single-cell dataset, and most of its bulk change survives composition adjustment (retained [gene=SDR16C5; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.66]). Missing are genetic or functional evidence, tractability data and any response-cohort signal; it is a hypothesis for experimental validation, not a target.

LAX1 is the top-scoring discovery candidate (up in five cohorts and antibody-tractable), but only a small part of its change survives composition adjustment (retained [gene=LAX1; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.23]). Single-cell data place it in plasma cells and T cells and the T/NK lineage does not replicate in the second dataset, so it mainly measures lymphocyte and plasma-cell infiltration. It would need a functional rationale in lymphocytes before being pursued.

CHRDL2 is stromal, mainly from inflammatory fibroblasts, with the lineage replicated in the second dataset, which makes it a candidate in the same cell state as MMP1 and CHI3L1. It is partly composition-driven and has appreciable RNA in a vital organ (max HPA nTPM [gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; vital_max_ntpm=42.6]), a safety question to resolve before considering it further.

ADGRG3 is classed by the screen as a first-in-class opportunity, but its transcripts are almost entirely neutrophil-derived (neutrophil share [gene=ADGRG3; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; neutrophil_share=0.906]), so like CXCR2 it reads out neutrophil abundance. It is a possible neutrophil-directed target only if a functional role is shown. XKR9, the remaining profiled candidate, is up in only two cohorts and its support is thin.

integration.text: The streams agree most on the neutrophil chemokine module: CXCR2, CXCR1 and CXCL8 are up in all five cohorts, local to inflamed mucosa, linked in STRING, supported by literature for CXCL8, carried by a neutrophil-to-neutrophil circuit that strengthens with inflammation, and, for CXCR2, backed by genetics and clinical-stage antagonists. They also agree that the epithelial metabolic and barrier losses (HMGCS2, SLC26A2, CLDN8) and calprotectin are robust biomarkers of local activity rather than targets. TNFa, NFkB and JAK-STAT activity and the JAK2 genetic signal coincide with the approved drug classes, a positive control for the approach.

The streams disagree on what the expression signal means. Cell-composition analysis shows that the top-ranked chemokine genes mostly measure neutrophil influx, and that CXCL8 and IL1B lose significance after adjustment, while expression alone would call them tissue changes. Genetics and expression barely overlap: most top expression genes (CXCL8, IDO1, MMP1, CHI3L1, DUOX2) have no genetic association, and the strongest genetic gene, IL23R, does not change. Literature favours CHI3L1, MMP1 and CXCL8, whereas CXCR2 has drugs and genetics but no extracted literature. Response data add a further caution: candidate markers of non-response mostly track severity in placebo arms.

limitations.text: All expression data are cross-sectional bulk biopsy transcriptomes; they show association, not causality, and microarray cohorts compress fold changes and have small control groups.

The convergence score rewards up-regulated genes; established targets whose mucosal expression does not change (TNF, JAK1, IL23R, integrins) are under-ranked, and genetics comes from Open Targets rather than fine-mapped UC loci.

Composition adjustment can over-correct when resident cells activate; losing significance is not proof of pure influx. Neutrophils are absent from Smillie 2019, so neutrophil-gene attributions rely on one dataset, and CXCR1, AQP9, CXCL1, MMP3, LCN2 and SLC26A2 were not composition-tested. Spatial data were not examined.

Ligand-receptor scores are co-expression, not signalling; pathway and TF activities are inferred from bulk and are confounded by cell composition. IL-23 and integrin pathways could not be assessed with PROGENy.

Response analyses are baseline and cross-sectional; infliximab, vedolizumab and golimumab arms are small, so null results there are weak, and most ustekinumab associations reflect severity seen in placebo.

Literature support comes from automated extraction over a limited corpus; several candidates (CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274) have no extracted relations, and much of the support is single-study or preclinical. Discovery candidates have no functional or genetic validation.

targets.rationale: First in the convergence ranking and the only top gene combining up-regulation in all five cohorts, local enrichment in inflamed mucosa, strong genetic association and clinical-stage antagonists (reparixin Phase 3). Its transcript is almost entirely neutrophil-derived and most of the bulk rise is neutrophil influx, so it is a target for blocking neutrophil recruitment; its association with ustekinumab non-response also appears in placebo, marking severity.

The CXCR2 ligand, up in all five cohorts with literature support for the CXCL8 neutrophil axis and only Phase 2 anti-IL-8 antibodies. Kept below CXCR2 because it has no genetic association and its bulk change loses significance after composition adjustment, so it is mainly a marker of neutrophil and myeloid influx.

Positive control: the JAK-inhibitor class is approved in UC, and JAK2 has a high Open Targets UC score while JAK-STAT activity and the STAT3 regulon are up in all five cohorts. Placed above the numeric ranking because its case rests on genetics and an approved mechanism, not on the modest biopsy change.

Up in all five cohorts and local to inflamed mucosa, stromal in single-cell data with the lineage replicated, genetically supported, with an antibody in clinical development (vixarelimab, Phase 2). The adjusted change is small, and the neutrophil OSM to fibroblast circuit does not strengthen with inflammation, which tempers the case.

Strongly induced in all five cohorts, made by macrophages and dendritic cells rather than neutrophils, with a significant change retained after composition adjustment and one preclinical study supporting IDO inhibition in colitis. Oncology inhibitors exist, but there is no genetic support and a repurposing case is a hypothesis.

A tissue-intrinsic inflammatory-fibroblast change that replicates across single-cell datasets and keeps a large adjusted change, with literature linking it to disease activity and anti-TNF response. Only broad MMP inhibitors exist, so it is ranked as a biomarker first and a selective-target hypothesis second.

One of the largest and most reproducible increases, from inflammatory fibroblasts, with a large change retained after adjustment and a shift already present in non-inflamed mucosa. Literature links it to macrophage pyroptosis, but there is no drug and no genetic support, so it is a strong biomarker and an untested target.

An epithelial-intrinsic induction (enterocytes, replicated, large adjusted change), up in all five cohorts and higher in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient; it marks epithelial oxidative and antimicrobial stress and has no drug.

Positive control for biomarkers: S100A8 is a subunit of calprotectin, the established stool activity marker. Up in all five cohorts and mostly neutrophil-derived, it measures neutrophil burden with some within-tissue induction.
Loss of epithelial ketogenesis, down in all five cohorts and unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa, so a clean marker of local inflammation; a lost function is not a druggable target.
The largest decrease in the meta-analysis, down in all five cohorts and lower in inflamed than non-inflamed mucosa; it marks barrier and absorptive-epithelium loss.

Up in all five cohorts with genetic support and a significant adjusted change, but spread across lineages and consistent with an inflammation-induced regulatory feedback. Placed below its numeric rank because existing PD-L1 drugs block the pathway, the wrong direction for UC; it is a marker of the interferon-driven response.

Exploratory: the cleanest first-in-class candidate, epithelial with the lineage replicated and most of its change retained after composition adjustment; it lacks genetic, functional and tractability evidence and needs experimental validation.

Exploratory: an inflammatory-fibroblast gene with replicated lineage, in the same cell state as MMP1 and CHI3L1; partly composition-driven and expressed in a vital organ, so safety must be resolved first.
